column4: The section’s j-z-y dictionary note gives “a father cannot repay for his child” as an example; this verse states that on the Day of Judgment neither parent nor child can avail the other, making that exact limit explicit in its own warning about the Day.

The section’s giver releases what he owns without seeking a return; this verse depicts people giving food to the poor, orphan, and captive. The next verse states their motive, but this verse contributes the concrete act of giving.

This verse calls wealth and children a trial and says great reward is with God. The following verse commands spending and guarding against the soul’s avarice, completing the contrast between possessions as a test and what brings success.

This verse likewise calls wealth and children a trial and says the great reward is with God. It gives another direct formulation of the section’s limit on treating possessions as personal sufficiency.
The section’s root ‘-s-r names both financial shortage and hardship; this verse uses its “difficult” form for the Day the Trumpet is blown, extending the word’s hardship sense to judgment.
The section glosses ‘-s-r through want and difficulty; this verse says that Day will not be easy for disbelievers, joining the same ease/difficulty axis to the fate beyond worldly wealth.

The section names r-d-y as ruin and links it to the moment when wealth cannot help; here Moses is warned not to follow desire and perish, giving the same root a moral downfall sense connected to turning away.
This verse says a person loves wealth intensely. It repeats the section’s specific image of attachment to possessions, also stated in 89:20, and explains the inward pull behind withholding them.
